Layout and ring-thickness experiment, 2026-10-21
The toolbar now offers exactly one layout algorithm: Force-directed. It uses Relational UI's existing d3-force dependency through a circle-layout export, with link attraction, Barnes–Hut repulsion and circle collision. Calculation runs in a browser worker with a fixed 120-step budget. Changing node or edge counts cancels obsolete calculations; component count and thickness changes preserve positions. This remains synthetic data with no engine discovery/query connection. Large layouts can take seconds; the toolbar and camera remain usable while calculating.
Ring px controls stroke thickness from 1 to 14 pixels at 100% zoom, default 5. The stroke's centreline radius is 14 pixels; maximum thickness leaves a 7-pixel inner radius. Thickness scales with zoom, and the layout reserves room for the maximum thickness. Rendering and pointer hit testing use the current outer radius.
The count and thickness spinboxes are native HTML number inputs, not reusable Relational UI spinbox components. The shared ViewPanel, ScrollArea and ZoomControl remain reused. Relational Engine owns data/query contracts, not browser input controls.

Previous exploration and verbatim discussion (historical evidence)
Successor to Analyze needs for the Graph editor. Begin after that task is complete. This is a sibling child under Develop the Graph editor view, outside the MVP.

Use the agreed needs and the verbatim interview recorded in the prerequisite task to run image-generation rounds with the user. Explore the Graph editor's 2D overview and focus presentations, node and relation information, filtering, navigation and layout.

Produce visual alternatives, collect the user's feedback and refine subsequent rounds. Preserve the generated images and decisions in this task's evidence and description. Distinguish exploratory mockups from accepted design. Do not silently settle the currently open graph scope, node content or layout questions through an image.

Outcome: a reviewed visual direction with remaining questions clearly identified, ready to guide implementation in the parent development task.

Deferred visual exploration from need analysis
The prerequisite interview's Answers 9 and 10 are the authoritative constraints and user direction for scalable node representation. The user is undecided about representations that change with zoom and asks to resolve this through image-generation experiments, not further abstract interview questions.

Explore concrete alternatives across comparable sparse and dense graph scenes and zoom levels. Include approaches with stable individual-node appearance as well as approaches whose representation changes with zoom; aggregation is a candidate to evaluate, not an accepted requirement. Other approaches remain open. Use the same underlying example data where possible so comparisons expose the design differences.

Evaluate the constraints recorded in Answer 9: very large numbers of varied nodes, a usable default without user-authored representation rules, and readability when zooming out. Do not assume a universal node label or show all node information by default. Preserve the agreed behavior for filtered endpoints while distinguishing it from any proposed aggregate.

Static images support decisions about visual hierarchy and readability. They do not establish interactive zoom behavior, layout stability, discovery completeness or runtime performance; identify any such questions requiring later interactive validation.

First-version scope
Follow the read-only scope agreed in Answer 11 of the prerequisite need-analysis task. Explore discovery, filtering, navigation and inspection. Creation, editing and deletion controls are outside these first-version mockups.

Initial query direction
Per Answer 17, show one unified filter expression composed from properties and Boolean operators. The prior example with separate startNodes/nodeFilter/edgeFilter groups was rejected and must not guide the mockups.
Follow Answers 12–15 and subsequent clarification in the prerequisite interview for the shared default filter and focus expression. Materialization is relative to an explicit engine instance, defaulting to the frontend instance. Focus starts from one or more selected nodes or a source-selection reference and includes directly connected materialized nodes, with all materialized edge types eligible. Express the neighborhood with maxTraversalDepth(1). Both incoming and outgoing edges are eligible by default; a separate operator can restrict direction, with its exact name and contract still open. Make these restrictions explicit through the filter. Do not imply that first opening discovers every available node. Per Answer 18, a filtered node can still be traversed to reach matching nodes. Every visible edge retains both endpoint representations, using shared Filtered placeholders where required. The depth restriction applies to nodes and edges. Edge-exclusion behavior and precise boundary-edge semantics remain under discussion.

Shared Query editor exploration
Include improvement of the existing Query editor component, as requested in Answer 18 of the prerequisite analysis. Compare concrete initial-state designs that avoid burdening the user with a prefilled expression while preserving access to and control of the initial filter.
Show how users discover active initial restrictions, inspect and modify them, and enter their own conditions within the same unified query. No arrangement is accepted yet. Do not hide an independently applied filter behind an apparently empty field or imply that removing visible conditions removes restrictions that remain inaccessible. These mockups guide reworking the shared component, not a bespoke graph-only replacement.

Query semantics and naming refinement
Follow Answer 19 in the prerequisite interview. The expression can contribute/select elements and restrict results; it is not exclusively a subtractive filter. Per Answer 20, use the accepted name Query editor for the existing shared component.
Keep the active initial query understandable and controllable. Removing materialized must not be depicted as an implicit request to search the entire graph recursively. The general expression-scoping model remains under discussion; visual designs must not silently settle it or split the unified expression into independent filters.

Operator-role presentation
Per Answer 20, make broad operator roles understandable within the unified expression. Explore the user's initial idea of green for additive, red for restrictive and possibly yellow for mutating roles. The taxonomy and colors are proposals to iterate on, not accepted final styling.
Explore how presentation communicates operator scope and effects while retaining the usable initial entry experience and access to the full effective query. Test ways to convey roles beyond color alone. A possible mutating category is an open future question and must not introduce graph mutation controls into the read-only first version.
Explicitness is a first protection against unintended work; mockups must not imply that deleting an explicit source silently triggers a recursive search across connected engines.

Query without a source
Follow Answer 23 of the prerequisite analysis: no source produces a valid query with an empty result in the first version. Do not present this case as a validation error or require the user to add a source. Preserve the prohibition on implicit recursive discovery.

RefreshRadioButton exploration
Follow Answer 24 of the prerequisite analysis. Include the requested reusable three-icon radio component named RefreshRadioButton: on demand, on demand with notification, automatic. Clicking either manual icon refreshes, even if its mode is already selected. Show a colored notification dot at the icon's top-right when a refresh is available in notification mode. Automatic mode refreshes the view itself. Per Answer 25, show on demand with notification as the default. The user delegates routine icon selection, selected-state styling, contextual help, notification-dot presentation and repeated-click details to the assistant. Handle these within the composed design without dedicated exploratory rounds or further questions. Static mockups cannot verify refresh activation or live change notification.

Apply and refresh
Per Answer 26 of the prerequisite analysis, show an explicit Apply button for edited queries. Distinguish the editable draft from the currently applied request sufficiently for users to understand what the graph represents. RefreshRadioButton governs updating results of the applied query and must not silently apply draft edits. Handle routine feedback details using existing shared UI conventions.

Iteration boundary
Per Answer 28 of the prerequisite analysis, do not include new contextual actions such as Show instances. Preserve the agreed initial queries and support manual query authoring with Apply.

Round 1: node representation across zoom
Begin the visual experiments with one comparison sheet: individual nodes at every zoom versus an explicitly grouped overview that restores individuals when zooming in. Use comparable illustrative topology and common close-up appearance to focus the comparison on zoom behavior. Keep the existing Node editor available for faithful inspection. Neither aggregation nor any specific visual mapping is accepted yet. Avoid universal node labels, application-domain special cases and invented automatic discovery. Later rounds can explore the initial-query UI and other visual questions.

Exact generation prompt
Use case: ui-mockup.
Create one polished, legible visual comparison sheet for an exploratory read-only desktop Graph editor in The Broccoli application. This is a design study, not a real product screenshot or performance result. Wide landscape image, clean flat software UI, no decorative lighting, no photographic perspective.
Composition: two equal columns labelled "A — Individual nodes" and "B — Grouped overview"; each column has two vertically stacked graph-canvas examples labelled "Closer" and "Further out". Both columns depict the same illustrative underlying graph and the same camera scales. The nearer examples show the SAME individual-node representation and comparable cropped region. The farther examples compare keeping individuals versus grouping. Reserve a narrow common panel at the right labelled "Node editor" showing the selected individual's underlying identity and components/relations, so faithful inspection remains accessible. This is a comparison sheet of canvas treatments, not four separate applications.
Visual style: match a compact dark technical desktop app: charcoal canvas, subdued broccoli-green header strips, thin neutral dividers, small clear sans-serif type. Restrained pale green, muted teal and warm amber marks; no strong glow, no gradients, no cards with paragraphs on the graph. Main title "Graph editor · Round 1". Small subtitle "Illustrative topology · Visual proposals".
Graph content: three uneven communities joined by sparse bridges, one highly connected hub and several sparse branches, varied but not a regular grid. Near views show about 35 nodes with individually traceable edges, slightly varied compact ring/segment glyphs, no text labels on ordinary nodes. One selected node has a crisp teal outline. A shared hollow neutral endpoint labelled "Filtered" has two visible edges converging on it; do not draw edges ending in empty space. These glyph/color mappings are exploratory, do not give them domain labels.
A farther view: show the wider graph with several hundred tiny individual glyphs, communities identifiable by spatial distribution but WITHOUT enclosing groups or substituting cluster nodes. Keep marks discernible. Naturally denser hubs may reveal legibility limits; do not fake an impossibly perfect sparse graph. Individual edges are fine muted strokes.
B farther view: same overall community locations, but explicitly grouped collections replace dense regions. Use visibly different aggregate glyphs, modest outlines/envelopes and small numeric member counts such as "38" and "64"; do not make a group look like an ordinary node. Keep sparse individual nodes visible. Show connections between groups with restrained bundled strokes. The matching nearer B view restores the individual nodes and their edges, demonstrating a candidate zoom-dependent representation.
Small common toolbar: "Graph editor", a compact "Query" disclosure with a visible scope summary "Frontend · Materialized", followed by three tiny mutually exclusive refresh icons with the middle selected and a small colored dot. Keep this toolbar identical for both concepts, with no large query panel competing with the graph. It is only surrounding context, not a proposed settled Query editor design. No hidden global scope, no automatic universal discovery, no contextual actions, no "Show instances", no edit/create/delete tools. Include a modest "Node editor" access indication.
Right inspector: selected node URL "graph://example/n42", section "Components" with two collapsed illustrative component rows and section "Relations" with two endpoint references. It is an identity/structure inspector, not a universal title source.
Text must be sparse and legible. Footer text exactly: "A keeps individual marks. B groups dense regions when zoomed out." Do not add charts, marketing copy, labels on every node, acceptance badges, or claims about measured scale. This sheet should make it possible to compare the two treatments visually without lengthy explanations.

Visual inspection notes
The output contains two matched close-up examples, an individual-node overview and a grouped overview, with a common inspector. Both preserve visible endpoint representations in the examples. Group envelopes, counts and some internal marks make the aggregate treatment visually distinct. The generated image is an illustration, not a deterministic rendering of shared graph data: counts and exact topology are not verified. Toolbar and inspector styling are surrounding mockup context, not accepted replacement components or validated implementations. In particular, the generated notification-dot placement does not establish the requested top-right position; implementation must follow the accepted requirement. Colors, glyph meanings, grouping method, layout and zoom behavior remain proposals. Static imagery cannot establish interactive stability, performance, query completeness or accessibility.

Exploratory visual rules
All ordinary nodes use equal-size circles. Component types are represented by equal contiguous colored ring sectors in stable type order; identical sets repeat the same pattern. Repeated instances do not add sectors. A no-component node uses a continuous neutral ring. Four illustrative type colors were used (teal, ochre, violet, pale blue); these are not accepted production assignments. Selection uses a separate white halo. Exact initial screenshot-edit prompt
Use case: precise-object-edit.
Asset type: single-viewport exploratory UI mockup, not a shipped graph renderer.
Input image 1 is the EDIT TARGET: the real empty Graph editor frame in The Broccoli app, 1480 by 764 pixels.
Preserve the existing app chrome exactly: the top breadcrumb/header row, its text and icons, the Graph editor selector and toolbar, margins, borders, colors and dimensions. Change ONLY the blank charcoal graph canvas rectangle x=2 to 1479, y=73 to 763. Do not add any toolbar, inspector, legend, title, caption, query field or inset. Keep ONE viewport at ONE zoom, no comparisons.

Within that rectangle draw a plausible flat 2D relational graph with about 85 individually visible nodes: three uneven connected neighborhoods, sparse bridges, a moderately dense hub, several branches, and a few isolated nodes. Apply these precise visual rules consistently:
1. Every ordinary node is the SAME small circle, about 16 pixels diameter, with charcoal center and a crisp 3-pixel segmented outer ring. Same size regardless of degree, importance, data size or component count. No text inside or beside ordinary nodes. No cards, icons for application domains, glow, shadows or 3D effects.
2. Ring segments represent DISTINCT COMPONENT TYPES carried by the node. A node with one type has one continuous color ring; two types produce equal half-rings, three equal thirds, four equal quarters. Tiny neutral gaps separate segments. Order segments clockwise by stable type identity, not position in the graph. Repeated component instances do not add segments. Equal component sets have exactly matching ring patterns wherever they occur. This scene contains four illustrative component types in this fixed order: type 1 muted teal #69BDB0, type 2 muted ochre #CEAC65, type 3 soft violet #AC94D0, type 4 pale blue #7FAAD0. Reuse those four types across ALL neighborhoods and mix common repeated patterns with some different combinations. Color does not encode status, priority, graph neighborhood or application domain.
3. Include three ordinary nodes with no components as thin continuous neutral gray rings, same diameter.
4. Mark exactly one ordinary node near the center-left as selected using a separate crisp WHITE outer halo, spaced 3 pixels beyond its colored ring. Keep its ring and size intact, no glow. Selection is not a fifth component color.
5. Include one excluded endpoint represented by a shared hollow neutral DASHED circle of the same diameter. Two visible edges terminate on this same placeholder. Put the single small neutral text 'Filtered' beside this endpoint; this is the only added text. Do not give it component colors or a selection halo.
6. Preserve the same flat dark app theme and charcoal canvas background from the reference. The graph should read as usable technical UI, not a decorative constellation. Show some natural edge crossings so the image honestly tests legibility.

This is a first visual experiment in component-composition rings. Do not invent category names, counts, explanatory annotations, zoom-dependent transitions or claims about scalability. Output only the edited screenshot with the original frame unchanged.

Visual correction
The first output repeated colors in some rings, weakening the rule of one sector per distinct type. A targeted correction was generated with this exact prompt:
Use case: precise-object-edit. Input is an exploratory Graph editor screenshot mockup.
Make ONE targeted correction: simplify and correct the node ring segments. Keep the existing app chrome, layout, nodes' positions, edge connections, selected white halo, Filtered placeholder and all text unchanged.
For each ordinary node use a circle with a charcoal center and ONE to FOUR large continuous colored arcs. Every color may appear ONLY ONCE on that circle. There are just four component colors: teal, ochre, violet and pale blue. One type = solid continuous full ring. Two types = two continuous equal semicircles. Three types = three continuous equal 120 degree arcs. Four types = four continuous equal quadrants. A 1 pixel charcoal separator only at each boundary between different types; absolutely no decorative dashes, repeated-color slices, alternating gray wedges or tiny extra segments. Consistent clockwise order teal then ochre then violet then pale blue, omitting absent types, beginning at 12 o'clock. Include many solid one-color rings and two-color half-rings, fewer three-color rings, and a few four-color rings. Repeat identical ring combinations at multiple positions. Component rings must be legible, flat and precise. Retain neutral no-component rings and the dashed Filtered endpoint unchanged.
All ordinary node bodies must remain the same small size. No new captions, inspector, legend, controls, zoom levels, glow, gradients, grouping envelopes or decoration. Preserve the original single viewport and screenshot frame.

Inspection and remaining limitations
The corrected image retains one viewport and the app frame, with simpler continuous rings, a separate selection halo and shared Filtered endpoint. It is illustrative raster output, not an exact rendering of a graph dataset; precise sector order and angle are not guaranteed by generation. The image does not prove scalability, accessibility, layout behavior or runtime performance. Many component types create palette collisions; many components on one node create unreadable sectors. Color patterns may support visual similarity but cannot uniquely identify arbitrary type sets. A future faithful Node editor remains necessary for exact inspection, as already required by the parent scope. The user has not accepted this visual direction. The parent development task records the completed frame validation and its limitations.

Round 3 direction
Record the user's concern that component-ring sectors will not scale when zooming out. Explore one zoomed-out viewport using solid marks with a minimum screen size. A color fingerprints the entire distinct-component set, rather than exposing each type through small sectors. Identical sets share color; palette collisions and dense spatial overlap remain limitations. This is an experiment, not an accepted replacement.

Exact prompt
Use case: precise-object-edit.
Input image 1 is the real empty Graph editor screenshot, 1480x764. Preserve the original app header, breadcrumb, icons, Graph editor selector, toolbar, borders and dark colors. Edit ONLY the blank graph canvas x=2..1479, y=73..763. One viewport, one zoom level. No inset, comparison, legend, caption, inspector or added controls.
Create a plausible zoomed-out overview of roughly 700 to 900 individual nodes, visible as SMALL SOLID CIRCULAR MARKS. Show one connected graph with four uneven dense neighborhoods, several sparse branches and bridges and a few isolated nodes. Give the communities organic irregular shapes, not stars, circles or symmetric blobs. Connections drive layout. Colors are thoroughly mixed throughout each community, not used to color whole communities. Keep all individuals; no aggregation, grouping envelopes, cluster icons or member counts.

Candidate display logic to illustrate:
- Every ordinary node is a solid circle, 4 screen pixels in diameter in the original 1480px reference size. Fixed minimum screen size preserves visibility when the camera zooms out. Degree, component count and importance do NOT change the mark size. No segmented rings, pies, inner marks, labels, outline details, glow or 3D.
- Each COMPLETE SET of distinct component types has one deterministic color fingerprint. Identical component sets repeat the same solid color throughout the entire graph, independent of position or community. Do not use majority component type. This scene uses six illustrative set fingerprints: muted teal #69BDB0, ochre #CEAC65, violet #AC94D0, blue #7FAAD0, pale rose #CE929B, soft green #99B77C. Plain gray denotes nodes without components. Colors indicate same composition, NOT status, importance or task domain. Palette collisions are a known limitation of this proposal, not something to disguise by inventing labels.
- Exactly one selected individual near the middle-left keeps its 4px filled mark and receives a separate crisp white selection ring, 12px outer diameter. Do not resize its node body.
- One shared filtered endpoint on a sparse bridge uses an 8px hollow dashed gray ring, with two edges ending on it and the small text Filtered beside it. It has no composition color. Only this state label is permitted.
- All edges are thin low-contrast neutral gray strokes ending on visible nodes or the filtered placeholder. Use a uniform subdued opacity; in dense neighborhoods the natural crossings are visible. Do not fake perfect readability by dropping most edges. Avoid thick bundled links or decorative constellations.
- The graph occupies the canvas broadly but keeps some breathing space. This is a realistic overview with a moderately congested central region and sparse periphery so we can assess the limitation of fixed minimum-size marks. Show slight crowding in the densest region, not perfectly spaced pseudo-data.

Flat technical app UI, restrained contrast, original charcoal canvas. No universal node text, no large floating node circles, no new UI chrome. Do not claim scalability or measured performance. This is an exploratory visual experiment, not an accepted specification. Output only the edited screenshot.

Visual inspection
The image retains the app frame and shows solid individual marks, a selection halo, a Filtered endpoint and visibly congested connected neighborhoods. It illustrates the tradeoff: minimum screen-size marks stay visible, but nodes and edges overlap in dense areas. Set fingerprints show matching combinations rather than revealing the individual types; they also do not preserve similarity between partly overlapping sets, and a finite palette cannot uniquely represent arbitrary sets. The six example colors are illustrative, not a selected production palette or accepted assignment algorithm. The generated node count, mark sizes and topology are not exact measured data. Scaling, exact identity, color accessibility and interaction remain unresolved. The user has not accepted this candidate.

Process correction
Stop generating further candidates now. The assistant changed encodings without first establishing the information the representation should help the user see. A deterministic mapping from component sets to color does not establish a useful visual purpose. Revisit the overview's intended information, the finite visual space, density handling, and the relationship between overview, query and faithful inspection before proposing another image. Neither segmented rings nor solid composition-color fingerprints is an accepted direction. Preserve the implemented empty frame and recorded evidence; the graph behavior and visual design remain unresolved.
